title: Agent Credentials vs. Human Credentials
summary: A human credential proves possession of two factors. An agent credential proves nothing about anyone. What RFC 8693's act claim, SPIFFE SVIDs and non-expiring service-account keys say about the difference.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**An agent credential and a human credential are different objects, and the standards say so in their own definitions. Treating them as one is why agent audit trails collapse under the question "who actually did this?"**


NIST SP 800-63B defines human authentication as verifying that a claimant "controls one or more authenticators" bound to a subscriber account, and requires "two distinct authentication factors" at AAL2. None of that applies to an agent. There is nobody to challenge, nothing to possess.


The instinct is to treat this as a logging problem that more monitoring would fix. It is an identity problem. RFC 8693 draws the line precisely: under impersonation the actor "is indistinguishable from B in that context", while under delegation "principal A still has its own identity separate from B". Hand an agent a person's login and you have chosen impersonation, and no amount of instrumentation recovers what the token threw away.


We are not arguing an agent needs human-shaped access. It needs narrower access that is unmistakably its own, and a record that names both parties.


The fix is cheap to start. Stop issuing keys that never expire, give the agent an identifier of its own, and make every call carry two subjects instead of one.
